{{short description|Collection of results for one-dimensional random walks and Brownian motion}}
In [[probability theory]], the '''arcsine laws''' are a collection of results for one-dimensional [[random walk]]s and Brownian motion (the [[Wiener process]]). The best known of these is attributed to {{harvs|txt|first=Paul|last=Lévy|authorlink=Paul Lévy (mathematician)|year=1939}}.

All three laws relate path properties of the Wiener process to the [[arcsine distribution]]. A random variable ''X'' on [0,1] is arcsine-distributed if

: <math>\Pr \left[ X \leq x \right] = \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin\left(\sqrt{x}\right), \qquad \forall x \in [0,1].
</math>

==Statement of the laws==
Throughout we suppose that (''W''<sub>''t''</sub>)<sub>0 &nbsp;≤&nbsp;''t''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;1</sub>&nbsp;&isin;&nbsp;'''R''' is the one-dimensional Wiener process on [0,1]. [[Wiener process#Self-similarity|Scale invariance]] ensures that the results can be generalised to Wiener processes run for ''t''&nbsp;&isin;[0,&infin;).

===First (Lévy's) arcsine law===
The first arcsine law states that the proportion of time that the one-dimensional Wiener process is positive follows an arcsine distribution. Let

: <math> T_+ = \left| \{\, t \in [0,1] \, \colon \, W_t > 0 \,\}\right| </math>

be the [[Lebesgue measure|measure]] of the set of times in [0,1] at which the Wiener process is positive. Then <math>T_+</math> is arcsine distributed.

===Second arcsine law===
The second arcsine law describes the distribution of the last time the Wiener process changes sign. Let

: <math>L=\sup\left\{t \in [0,1] \, \colon \, W_t = 0 \right\} </math>

be the time of the last zero. Then ''L'' is arcsine distributed.

===Third arcsine law===
The third arcsine law states that the time at which a Wiener process achieves its maximum is arcsine distributed.

The statement of the law relies on the fact that the Wiener process has an almost surely unique maxima,<ref name="Morters_Peres">Morters, Peter and Peres, Yuval, ''Brownian Motion'', Chapter 2.</ref> and so we can define the random variable ''M'' which is the time at which the maxima is achieved. i.e. the unique ''M'' such that

: <math> W_M = \sup \{ W_s \, \colon \, s \in [0,1] \}. </math>

Then ''M'' is arcsine distributed.

==Equivalence of the second and third laws==
Defining the running maximum process ''M''<sub>''t''</sub> of the Wiener process

: <math> M_t = \sup \{ W_s \, \colon \, s \in [0,t] \}, </math>

then the law of ''X''<sub>''t''</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''M''<sub>''t''</sub>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''W''<sub>''t''</sub> has the same law as a reflected Wiener process |''B''<sub>''t''</sub>| (where ''B''<sub>''t''</sub> is a Wiener process independent of ''W''<sub>''t''</sub>).<ref name="Morters_Peres" />

Since the zeros of ''B'' and |''B''| coincide, the last zero of ''X'' has the same distribution as ''L'', the last zero of the Wiener process. The last zero of ''X'' occurs exactly when ''W'' achieves its maximum.<ref name="Morters_Peres" /> It follows that the second and third laws are equivalent.
